observation.visible_scene: First-person point-of-view shot from the nose of a white surfboard (black stringer visible) floating in turquoise ocean water. A breaking wave with whitewater foam sits ahead in the center-left. The background shows a coastline on the left with high-rise buildings and a tree-covered rocky headland, a line of distant surfers on the right, and a blue sky with scattered clouds. The whole frame is rolled/tilted, so the horizon runs diagonally.
visible_changes: The surfboard nose, prominent at the bottom in frames 1-20, progressively shrinks and drops out of the bottom edge by about frame 26-30 as the camera orientation changes relative to the board.
The patch of breaking-wave foam in the center of the frame grows from a thin line at mid-distance into a broad churned expanse of whitewater filling the lower half of the view by the end.
The viewpoint advances toward that foam; the foam texture continuously churns and spreads rather than translating as a rigid object.
The horizon tilt/roll changes throughout the excerpt (a strong diagonal slope early, a more level orientation mid-clip, tilting again later), indicating camera rotation.
Water droplets appear on the lens and multiply/enlarge toward the final frames (39-41), increasingly obscuring the scene.
The line of surfers on the right stays roughly in place relative to the horizon, shifting slightly in frame position without changing their spacing.
The buildings and rocky headland on the left remain fixed landmarks, sliding slowly as the camera rolls and moves forward.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the rider catches the wave, is engulfed by the foam, or paddles over it after this segment ends.
The exact cause of the droplets on the lens (wave spray vs. an unseen impact).
What paddling or motion preceded the start of this cropped excerpt.
uncertain_details: Whether the board nose leaving the frame is due to the camera pitching up or the board dipping, as both are consistent with the frames.
The precise split between camera roll and camera pitch given the persistently tilted horizon.
Whether the foam's growth is the wave breaking/expanding or mainly the viewpoint closing in on it.
